property_summary: For every caller, the correct contract's owner() returns the stored owner address (not the zero address); the mutant returns address(0) breaking this invariant for some inputs (any caller where stored owner != address(0)).

For every caller address, the deployed reference contract's owner() returns the stored non-zero owner (the deployer) while the mutant returns address(0), so the general rule is that owner() != address(0) for the deployed contract and the mutant violates this for all callers (some input), observed via calling owner().

For any caller address, the deployed correct contract reports a non-zero owner via owner(), while the mutant returns the zero address; thus owner() != address(0) always holds for the reference but is violated by the mutant for callers when the stored owner is non-zero.

For every caller, the deployed reference contract's owner() call returns a non-zero address (the stored owner), whereas the mutant returns address(0); thus assertTrue(owner() != address(0)) holds for all inputs on the reference and is broken by the mutant for some input.

For every caller, the reference contract's owner() returns a non-zero address (the deployed owner), whereas the mutant returns address(0) breaking the invariant owner() != address(0) for some inputs; the test asserts that owner() != address(0).

For any caller, the owner() view always returns the stored owner address (the deployer set in constructor); the mutant that returns msg.sender will return a different value for some caller (e.g. any address not equal to the stored owner), breaking this property.

For any caller, the reference contract's owner() view always returns the stored deployer (the contract owner); the mutant that returns _msgSender() will for some callers return a different address, so owner() != caller can be observed for those inputs.
For every caller address A, C.owner() returns the fixed stored owner (the deployer); the mutant that returns _msgSender() will return A for some A ≠ stored owner, violating this invariant.

For every caller address, the reference contract's owner() returns the fixed deployed owner address (the deployer); the mutant that returns _msgSender() will for some caller addresses return a different value, so owner() equals the deployer for all callers in the correct contract but not in the mutant.

For every caller address A, the reference contract's owner() returns the fixed stored deployer address (the owner) while the mutant that returns _msgSender() will for some caller addresses return A instead, so the universal property is: owner() equals the deployer for all callers; the mutant violates this for callers not equal to the deployer.

For any caller, the correct contract's owner() always returns the stored owner address (the deployer set in constructor), whereas the mutant returning tx.origin can differ when called via an intermediate contract (tx.origin is the original EOA), so calling owner() through a contract proxy yields different results between P and M.

For any caller (EOA or contract), the reference contract's owner() returns the stored owner address (the deployer), but the mutant that returns tx.origin can return a different address when owner() is invoked via an intermediate contract (i.e., when msg.sender != tx.origin), so the property is: owner() == deployer for all callers — the mutant violates this for some caller contracts.

For every caller, the original contract's owner() always returns the deployer address stored at construction; the mutant that returns tx.origin can return a different address when owner() is invoked via a contract (tx.origin != deployer), so the mutant violates this universal property for some caller contract.

For every caller (EOA or contract), the reference contract's owner() always returns the stored owner (the deployer); the mutant that returns tx.origin can return a different address when owner() is invoked via a contract that itself was called by a different EOA, so there exists a caller contract + tx.origin where owner() differs.

For every caller, C.owner() always returns the stored deployer address (the owner set in the constructor); the mutant returning tx.origin can return a different address when invoked through an intermediate contract (tx.origin differs), so there exists a caller contract and EOA origin that make owner() return a different value.

Invariant: transferOwnership(newOwner) always reverts (fails) when newOwner == address(0) (reference enforces non-zero new owner), but the mutant allows setting owner to address(0) so the call succeeds for newOwner == address(0).

In the reference contract, transferOwnership(address(0)) is forbidden (the call reverts), so for every address input the call succeeds iff the address is non-zero; the mutant removes the zero-address check so calling transferOwnership(address(0)) can succeed — the property: calling transferOwnership with a fuzzy address must revert exactly when the address is zero (reference) and the mutant will allow success for address(0).

Invariant: transferOwnership(newOwner) reverts when called with newOwner == address(0) (reference enforces non-zero new owner), so for any fuzzed address the call's success boolean equals (newOwner != address(0)); the mutant removing the zero-address check will make the call succeed for address(0), violating this rule for that input.

For all addresses newOwner the reference C's transferOwnership(newOwner) call succeeds iff newOwner != address(0) (it must revert for address(0)); the mutant removing the zero-address check will allow transferOwnership(address(0)) to succeed, violating this rule for that input.

The reference contract's transferOwnership(newOwner) call must revert when newOwner == address(0) (owner cannot be set to zero); the mutant removing that require allows transferOwnership(address(0)) to succeed, violating this rule for that input.

For any caller address X, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) when X is the current owner must succeed (reference uses owner() accessor); the mutant that compares msg.sender directly to internal _owner can be broken if owner() is overridden (so transferOwnership may wrongly revert for some callers that owner() would accept).

For any caller address X, if owner() returns X then transferOwnership(X_new) must succeed (reference uses owner() accessor); the mutant compares msg.sender to internal _owner directly so an override of owner() can make owner() == X while _owner != X, causing transferOwnership to revert for some callers.

For any caller, if owner() reports the caller as owner then transferOwnership(...) succeeds; the mutant compares msg.sender to the internal _owner directly (bypassing owner()), so when owner() is overridden to report a different address the reference allows transferOwnership but the mutant may reject it.

For any address reported as owner() by a contract that overrides Ownable.owner(), calling transferOwnership(...) while impersonating that reported owner must succeed on the reference implementation, but the mutant that compares msg.sender to the internal _owner directly can revert for some overriding owners; the test fuzzes an overriding owner address and newOwner to find such a case.

If owner() (the public accessor) reports that the caller is the owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) must succeed (reference); the mutant which compares msg.sender to the internal _owner directly can revert when owner() is overridden to report a different address — so the property is: for any newOwner and any overriding-owner contract X where X.owner() == X (i.e. the contract reports itself as owner) a call routed through X to transferOwnership should succeed on the reference but may fail on the mutant.

For any caller address X and any _operator address O, when the owner calls setOperator(O) the contract's operator getter must equal O afterwards; the mutant that omits the assignment will emit the event but leave operator unchanged, violating this property for some inputs.

For any owner caller and any address arg, after calling setOperator(arg) the contract's operator() must equal that arg; the mutant that removes the assignment still emits the event but leaves operator unchanged, so operator() != arg for some inputs.

For any owner caller and any address arg, after calling setOperator(arg) the contract's operator() getter returns arg; the mutant that omits the assignment still emits the event but leaves operator unchanged, so operator() != arg for some inputs.

For any address newOp and any caller who is the contract owner, calling setOperator(newOp) results in c.operator() == newOp afterwards; the mutant that removes the assignment will leave operator unchanged for some newOp, breaking this property.

For any owner caller and any address newOperator, after calling setOperator(newOperator) the contract's operator() getter equals newOperator; the mutant that removes the assignment will sometimes leave operator() unchanged, violating this rule.

For any input address newOp provided to setOperator by the owner, the reference contract sets operator to that exact address (operator == newOp); the mutant instead always sets operator to owner(), so there exist inputs where operator != newOp and the property is violated.

For any address X passed to setOperator by the owner, the reference contract sets operator() == X after the call; the mutant instead sets operator() == owner(), so for at least some X (X != owner()) the mutant violates this.

For every address newOp passed to setOperator by the owner, the reference contract sets operator() equal to newOp; the mutant instead always sets operator() to owner(), so when newOp != owner() the mutant violates this rule.

For every address newOp provided to setOperator by the contract owner, the reference contract sets operator() == newOp; the mutant instead sets operator() == owner(), so when newOp != owner() the mutant violates this rule.

For any address newOp supplied by the contract owner to setOperator, the correct contract sets operator() to that supplied newOp; the mutant instead sets operator() to owner(), so when newOp != owner() the mutant violates this rule.

After calling setOperator(x) the stored operator equals the provided address x (i.e. operator == x) in the correct contract for every input; the mutant that stores the bitwise NOT of x will violate this for any x where ~x != x (some inputs).

For every input address a, after calling setOperator(a) the contract's public operator() getter must equal the provided address a; the mutant stores bitwise NOT of a so for some a (those where ~a != a) operator() will differ and the assertion fails.

For every address input a, calling setOperator(a) results in operator() returning exactly the provided address a in the correct contract; the mutant inverts the bits of a before storing so for some a the stored operator differs and the property is violated.

For every address a, after calling setOperator(a) the contract's public operator() equals the provided a; the mutant that stores bitwise-NOT(~a) will cause operator() != a for some a, so the property holds for the reference and is violated by the mutant for those inputs.

For every provided address a, after calling setOperator(a) the contract's public operator() getter returns exactly the provided address a; the mutant stores the bitwise NOT of a so for some a the getter will differ and the property is violated.

For every caller address x, calling setOperator(x) as owner must succeed and set operator==x in the reference; the mutant inverts the onlyOwner check so an actual owner call will revert and operator will not be set for some fuzzed owner addresses.

For any caller who is the contract owner, calling setOperator(newOperator) always succeeds on the correct contract and sets operator == newOperator; the mutant inverts the onlyOwner check so when the owner calls setOperator it will revert (or fail to set operator) for some fuzzed newOperator values.

For any caller who is the contract owner, calling setOperator(newOperator) on the correct contract always succeeds and sets operator() == newOperator; the mutant inverts onlyOwner so owner calls will revert (or fail) and thus for some fuzzed newOperator values the mutant will not set operator() to that value.

For any caller that is the contract owner, calling setOperator(newOperator) MUST succeed (not revert) and set operator() to newOperator; the mutant inverts onlyOwner so owner calls can revert and thus will not set operator(), so there exist owner / newOperator inputs where the mutant fails while the reference succeeds.

For any caller who is the contract owner, calling setOperator(newOperator) always succeeds on the correct contract and sets operator() == newOperator; the mutant inverts the onlyOwner check so when the owner calls setOperator the call will revert (or not set operator) for some fuzzed newOperator values.

For any caller owner invoking setOperator(x), the contract's operator becomes exactly the provided argument x in the reference; the mutant instead sets operator = tx.origin, so there exist calls where operator != x (e.g., when owner calls via a contract), violating the rule.

For any address _operator and any caller that is the contract owner making the call via an intermediate contract, the reference sets operator to the provided _operator; the mutant incorrectly sets operator to tx.origin (the intermediate contract's caller) and thus can differ when owner calls through a contract.

For any address newOp and any owner-invoked call to setOperator routed through an intermediary contract, the correct contract sets operator() == newOp (uses the provided argument) while the mutant sets operator() == tx.origin (breaking this rule when the owner calls via a contract), so operator equals the passed parameter for all such calls in the reference but not in the mutant.

When the contract owner calls setOperator(via any caller), the correct contract always sets operator() equal to the function argument provided; the mutant that uses tx.origin can differ when the owner calls through an intermediate contract, so operator() != provided argument for some inputs.

For any address newOperator and any owner caller that invokes setOperator(newOperator) (even when calling through an intermediate contract), the reference contract sets operator() == newOperator; the mutant that uses tx.origin can produce operator() != newOperator when the owner calls via a forwarding contract.
